strengths: The core idea is simple, intuitive, and clearly explained: replacing a single global scale-and-shift with a flexible, radar-predicted polynomial transform is a reasonable and lightweight way to adapt frozen MDE predictions to metric scale.

The empirical evaluation is broad: three datasets (nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, View-of-Delft) and four MDE backbones (DPT, Depth Anything, Depth Pro, UniDepth), with consistent improvements over RadarCam-Depth and other radar-camera baselines.

The first-derivative monotonicity regularizer is a sensible safeguard against oscillatory high-degree polynomials, and the degree-sensitivity study (Table 3) and component ablations (Table 4) give some insight into what matters.
The qualitative comparison (Fig. 3) and the inflected-polynomial visualization (Fig. 4) help communicate the intended behavior, and the claimed computational overhead is modest.
The framing of metric depth estimation as a scene-fitting problem is a fresh perspective relative to completion- or confidence-driven fusion pipelines.
weaknesses: Conceptual mismatch at the heart of the motivation. The predicted map is d = sum_i c_i z^i, applied pointwise as a function of the scaleless depth z, and the loss explicitly enforces d d/dz ~ 1 (monotonic). A deterministic monotonic remapping of z cannot fix *ordinal* misorderings between objects (points with the same z map to the same d, and ordering is preserved). Yet Fig. 1 and Sec. 3.1 repeatedly frame the failure mode as objects placed at 'incorrect relative depths' and 'cross-object misalignments.' The paper conflates magnitude/ratio errors with ordering errors, which weakens the central claim that inflection points 'correct misalignments.'

Tension between the monotonicity loss and the claimed benefit. Forcing the derivative close to 1 constrains the transform to be nearly a shift (d ~ z + c), directly limiting the 'non-uniform stretching/compressing' that is advertised as the key advantage. The trade-off governed by lambda_3 is neither quantified nor analyzed.

Inconsistent improvement numbers. The abstract claims 30.3% MAE / 37.2% RMSE, the introduction claims 11.3% / 54.6% / 35.2%, and Table 1 implies yet other values (e.g., ~11% MAE on nuScenes, ~46% MAE on ZJU). The abstract's headline figure also appears to be measured against raw MDE rather than 'existing methods,' which is misleading. These must be reconciled and stated transparently.

Missing critical baseline. The paper never compares against a generic learned monotonic mapping (MLP/spline/isotonic regression) from z to metric depth, nor against a per-dataset global polynomial fit. Without this, it is impossible to tell whether the *polynomial parameterization* or simply *any* flexible nonlinear mapping drives the gains, so the claimed novelty is not isolated.

Limited novelty. Learned nonlinear heads converting relative/scaleless depth to metric depth are well established (e.g., ZoeDepth-style heads), and prototype/cross-attention fusion and radar aggregation are standard. The genuinely new element—predicting polynomial coefficients from radar—is incremental, and the claim of being the 'first to formulate radar-camera depth estimation as a scene-fitting problem' is strong and unsupported.

Reproducibility gaps in the main text. Loss weights (lambda_1, lambda_2, lambda_3), the polynomial degree used for the main results, training schedule, dataset splits, and the units of the reported MAE/RMSE (values in the thousands are unexplained) are all deferred to an unseen supplement, making the results hard to verify.
The prototypical aggregation and cross-modal attention are presented as components without clear justification that they are necessary or better than simpler pooling, beyond a single ablation line.

strengths: Simple, well-motivated core idea: replacing the standard global linear scale-and-shift transformation with radar-guided polynomial fitting directly targets the documented failure mode of cross-object relative-depth misalignments that a single scale factor cannot fix (Fig. 1 provides a clean illustration).

Consistent, measurable gains across three datasets (nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, View-of-Delft) and all three evaluation ranges (50/70/80 m), with PolyRad outperforming all five baselines in Table 1, supporting the central claim.

The first-derivative monotonicity regularization (Eq. 8-9) is principled and well-justified: it prevents higher-order polynomials from inverting local depth ordering or oscillating, which is a genuine failure mode of high-degree fits, and the ablation (Table 4) confirms its contribution.

Ablations are reasonably complete: learnable prototypes vs. self-attention, cross-modality fusion, and the monotonicity loss are each isolated, and the polynomial-degree sensitivity study (Table 3) gives practical guidance and shows a sensible optimum around degree 6-8.

The geometric framing via inflection points (Eq. 2) gives interpretable intuition for why non-uniform corrections are needed, and the method adds negligible computational cost over the linear baseline.

Comparative study across four MDE backbones (Table 2) shows the polynomial transform consistently improves over RadarCam-Depth with the same backbone, isolating the method's contribution from the backbone.
weaknesses: Reported improvement numbers are inconsistent across the paper: the abstract states 30.3% MAE / 37.2% RMSE, the introduction states 11.3%/54.6%/35.2%, and Section 4.1 states 12.1%/10.5% (nuScenes), 46.8%/62.4% (ZJU), 31.8%/38.5% (VoD). These do not reconcile, which weakens confidence in the headline claims and should be corrected.

The polynomial degree N is treated as a dataset-dependent hyperparameter requiring per-dataset tuning (acknowledged in Limitations); no adaptive selection mechanism is proposed, limiting practical deployment.

There is a conceptual tension the paper only partially addresses: the polynomial is introduced to allow flexible non-uniform corrections, yet the monotonicity regularizer pushes the first derivative toward 1, which constrains exactly the flexibility being exploited. The paper does not quantify how much of the achievable correction is forfeited by this constraint.

Effectiveness depends heavily on the frozen MDE backbone: with DPT as backbone the raw polyfit result (1525.6 MAE) is worse than several baselines using stronger backbones, and the paper does not analyze when polynomial fitting fails to recover misalignments.

The method is an incremental extension of the scale-and-shift paradigm; while the radar-guided coefficient prediction and monotonicity loss are reasonable engineering contributions, the core conceptual novelty is moderate.

The claim that radar points provide 'metric depth measurements' is somewhat loose given the paper itself emphasizes radar sparsity and noise (elevation ambiguity, multipath); a clearer statement of how metric supervision actually enters (through the ground-truth loss, not through the radar features) would help.

Qualitative comparisons (Fig. 3) rely on a small number of hand-picked samples; no failure-case analysis or per-region error breakdown is provided to substantiate the cross-object-misalignment narrative beyond aggregate MAE/RMSE.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated core idea: replacing the ubiquitous linear scale-and-shift transformation with a learned polynomial transformation that introduces inflection points, enabling non-uniform, depth-dependent corrections that cannot be achieved by a single global scale factor. The motivation (Fig. 1, Sec. 3.1) is clean and persuasive.

Clear theoretical framing: the argument that polynomial fitting provides a principled middle ground between per-pixel regression (ill-posed given only hundreds of radar points) and a two-parameter linear fit (over-constrained) is well articulated, and the degree-of-freedom reasoning is a genuinely useful conceptual contribution.

The monotonicity regularization via a first-derivative term (Eq. 8-9) is a simple, well-justified mechanism to prevent the higher-order polynomial from introducing spurious non-monotonic depth reversals, and the ablation (Tab. 4) shows it materially helps.

Comprehensive empirical validation: three datasets (nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, View-of-Delft), three evaluation distances (50/70/80m), five baselines, four MDE backbones (Tab. 1-2), a polynomial-degree sensitivity study (Tab. 3), and component ablations (Tab. 4). The degree-1 vs. degree-8 gap in Tab. 3 directly supports the central hypothesis.
Practical efficiency: predicting N+1 coefficients instead of per-pixel corrections adds negligible compute, which is a real advantage over heavier completion-style architectures.

Qualitative results (Fig. 3) show concrete failure modes of baselines (omitted structures, misplaced objects) that PolyRad corrects, and Fig. 4 nicely visualizes how increasing polynomial degree reduces error.
weaknesses: Inconsistent reporting of improvement percentages across sections. The abstract claims 30.3% MAE / 37.2% RMSE, the introduction lists 11.3% / 54.6% / 35.2%, and Sec. 4.1 states 12.1% / 10.5% (nuScenes), 46.8% / 62.4% (ZJU), 31.8% / 38.5% (VoD). While these may reflect different baselines and averaging schemes, the paper never states which baseline each figure is relative to, making the headline numbers hard to verify and undermining confidence in the reported gains.

No empirical comparison against alternative non-linear transformation families (e.g., monotonic splines, isotonic regression, monotonic MLPs) that also provide more than two degrees of freedom. Such a comparison would be needed to justify the specific choice of a polynomial basis rather than a more general monotone mapping.

The global-per-scene polynomial applies a single transformation as a function of depth value only; the paper does not analyze cases where MDE errors are spatially varying at equal depth, which would be a natural limitation of the parameterization.

Many essential implementation details (λ1/λ2/λ3 weights, training schedule, network dimensions, prototype count, degree selection procedure) are deferred entirely to the Supp. Mat., leaving the main paper under-specified for reproduction.

The polynomial degree is acknowledged as a per-dataset hyperparameter (Sec. 5), and the optimal degree differs across datasets; the paper does not describe a principled, data-driven selection rule, which weakens the claim of generalizability.

The monotonicity term enforces the derivative to be close to 1 (not merely non-negative), which is a stronger constraint than monotonicity and could limit the achievable correction; the target value and the trade-off weight λ3 are not ablated in the main text.

strengths: Novel and conceptually clean idea: replacing the standard affine (scale-and-shift) calibration of scale-less MDE predictions with a learned polynomial transformation, which is well-motivated by the observation that affine transforms cannot reconcile three or more misaligned regions. The framing as a 'scene-fitting' problem is fresh and the insight is transferable.

Theoretical grounding is provided via Proposition 1 (Appendix H), a constructive proof that no global affine transform can fit k>=3 misaligned (MDE, GT) pairs, plus the Corollary arguing polynomial/Taylor expansions can approximate the relationship arbitrarily well. This gives the method a principled justification beyond empirical tuning.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: three datasets (nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, View-of-Delft), multiple max-distance thresholds (50/70/80m), comparisons against strong and recent baselines (RadarNet, SparseBeatsDense, GET-UP, RadarCam-Depth, TacoDepth), plus depth-completion methods (NLSPN, BPNet) and adapter/regression baselines (LoRA, ViT-Adapter, isotonic regression, splines).

Efficiency is a genuine strength: 24.81 ms/frame (40+ fps), 89.70 GFLOPs, and the lowest per-epoch training time (33.16 min), with the appendix showing each added polynomial degree incurs only a 0.0048% FLOP increase. This makes the method practically deployable, unlike heavier fusion alternatives.

Well-designed ablations: polynomial degree sweep (Table 5), component ablation (Table 6), MDE backbone comparisons (Tables 4, 9, 10), zero-shot cross-dataset generalization (Table 11), radar point density robustness (Table 12), and a monotonicity/Kendall-tau analysis with bootstrap t-test (p=0.012). The degree=1 (scale+shift) row cleanly isolates the benefit of the polynomial formulation.

The first-derivative monotonicity regularizer is a sensible and necessary design choice for stabilizing high-degree polynomial fits, and its removal is shown to degrade performance (Table 6), validating the motivation about avoiding harmful non-monotonic oscillations.
weaknesses: Numerical inconsistency in headline claims: the abstract states an average improvement of '24.9% in MAE and 33.2% in RMSE,' while the Introduction claims '29.1%,' and Section 4.1 reports per-dataset figures (4.4%/3.7% on nuScenes, 38.5%/57.5% on ZJU, 31.8%/38.5% on VoD). These numbers should be reconciled and their averaging defined, since the reader cannot easily tell which comparison baseline or aggregation is being used.

The gains on nuScenes—the most established benchmark—are modest (MAE 1014.4 vs. TacoDepth 1046.8 at 50m, a ~3% relative improvement), and the largest improvements appear on ZJU and VoD. This weakens the 'state-of-the-art across the board' framing somewhat; the paper would benefit from a clearer discussion of why the advantage is benchmark-dependent.

The polynomial degree is a dataset-dependent hyperparameter (degree 8 best on nuScenes, degree 6 on ZJU), and performance degrades at degree 10. This is acknowledged as a limitation, but no principled selection criterion (e.g., validation-based or adaptive) is offered, leaving a practical tuning burden and some concern about robustness of the reported optimum.

It is not fully disentangled how much of the gain comes from the polynomial fitting versus the radar-aggregation/prototype and fusion design. The component ablation helps, but a direct comparison where the identical fusion architecture predicts only 2 affine coefficients versus N+1 polynomial coefficients (beyond the degree=1 row) would more cleanly isolate the contribution of the polynomial head itself.

The radar point clouds used are extremely sparse (~97 points on nuScenes, ~276 on VoD, ~465 on ZJU) relative to ~10^6 pixels. The paper argues the problem is better posed than pixel-wise regression, but it does not quantify how sensitive the learned polynomial coefficients are to radar noise, outliers, or multipath—despite motivating prototypes partly on this basis.

Some qualitative and quantitative claims (e.g., 'state-of-the-art in both performance and efficiency') rely on a specific, potentially favorable set of baselines; the paper does not report variance/error bars for the main depth metrics across runs, making it hard to assess whether small margins (e.g., nuScenes) are statistically meaningful.

strengths: The core insight is original and well-motivated: the paper correctly identifies that scale ambiguity in monocular depth estimation (MDE) is not reducible to a single global scale-and-shift once three or more regions are misaligned, and formalizes this with a constructive proof (Proposition 1, Appendix H) showing no affine transform can fit such point sets. This elevates the contribution from a heuristic to a principled formulation.

The polynomial-fitting formulation (predicting N+1 coefficients that reshape the scaleless depth map) is a clean, well-posed middle ground between over-determined affine fitting (2 DOF) and under-determined per-pixel mapping (~10^6 DOF). The geometric intuition about inflection points and the depth-dependent correction mechanism is clearly explained.

The first-derivative monotonicity regularizer (Eq. 6-7) is a novel and appropriate inductive bias that directly addresses the known oscillatory failure mode of high-degree polynomial fitting, and the ablation (Tab. 6) shows it matters. The Kendall's tau analysis (Appendix G) provides quantitative evidence that the regularization preserves ordinality.

Empirical results are strong and consistent: SOTA MAE/RMSE on nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, and View-of-Delft across 50/70/80 m thresholds, with a full benchmark table (Tab. 7) including depth-completion baselines (NLSPN, BPNet) that are shown to fail on sparse radar.

The efficiency claims are well-supported (Tab. 2, 3): lowest training time (33.16 min/epoch), lowest inference latency (24.81 ms, >40 fps), and lowest GFLOPs (89.70), with a clear derivation of the negligible per-degree overhead in Appendix B.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for a method paper: four MDE backbones (Tab. 4, 9, 10), degree sensitivity (Tab. 5), architecture/loss ablations (Tab. 6), zero-shot cross-dataset generalization (Tab. 11), reduced radar density robustness (Tab. 12), and comparisons to adapters and classical regression baselines (Tab. 13).
The manuscript is clearly written, figures are informative (Fig. 1, 2, 3, 4, 6), and the design choices (learned prototypes for radar aggregation, soft cross-modal fusion) are explained and ablated.
weaknesses: The polynomial degree is a dataset-dependent hyperparameter (degree 8 best on nuScenes/ZJU, degree 6 near-optimal, degradation at degree 10). This requires per-dataset tuning and somewhat weakens the 'out-of-the-box' appeal, though the authors acknowledge it as a limitation and show a plateau between degrees 6-8.

The claim that 'the number of degrees of freedom in polynomial expansion... is close to the cardinality of radar point clouds' is not supported by the reported numbers: the method uses ~8-10 coefficients, whereas nuScenes/ZJU/VoD frames contain ~97/465/276 radar points. The middle-ground argument remains valid, but this specific justification overstates the correspondence.

Headline improvement figures vary across the paper (abstract: 24.9% MAE / 33.2% RMSE average; contributions: 29.1%; Sec. 4.1: 4.4% MAE on nuScenes). While the abstract's averaged numbers are arithmetically consistent with the per-dataset results, the differing figures without explicit aggregation definitions could confuse readers; the nuScenes gain (4.4% MAE) is notably modest relative to the quoted averages.

The method is fundamentally bounded by the frozen MDE backbone; there is no analysis of failure cases where the MDE prior is structurally wrong (e.g., severe occlusions or out-of-distribution scenes), nor of behavior when radar is unavailable or severely degraded. Tab. 12 covers density reduction but not radar dropout/outage.

Several architectural components (prototype-based soft clustering, cross-modal attention-style fusion, GAP-based coefficient prediction) are standard building blocks; the novelty rests primarily on the polynomial formulation and the monotonicity regularizer rather than the fusion design.

The monotonicity regularizer enforces dd/dz ≈ 1 globally rather than only within local regions/objects; the paper motivates this with an intra-object argument but the loss is applied over the whole map, which could over-constrain legitimate cross-region corrections. No ablation isolates this effect.

Reported cropped camera resolutions (300x1280, 608x1936) suggest evaluation on lidar-reprojected regions only; it is not fully clear how much of the image is scored and whether the modest nuScenes numbers are partly due to saturation or to evaluation-region differences.

strengths: The core formulation is simple and cheap: replacing the affine scale-and-shift head used in prior radar–camera metric depth work with a learned (N+1)-parameter polynomial recalibration adds negligible overhead, and the efficiency results (Tab. 2: 33.16 min/epoch; Tab. 3: 24.81 ms, 40.3 fps, 89.70 GFLOPs) support the practical-deployment claim, which is genuinely relevant for autonomous driving.

The empirical package is broad and mostly well-executed: three datasets (nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, View-of-Delft) at 50/70/80 m thresholds, qualitative comparisons on two datasets, and an unusually complete appendix (degree sensitivity in Tab. 5, component/loss ablations in Tab. 6, comparisons against isotonic regression, cubic Hermite spline, PCHIP, LoRA and ViT-Adapter in Tab. 13, zero-shot cross-dataset transfer in Tab. 11, reduced radar density in Tab. 12).

Several analyses are informative and would be useful to the community if the numbers were reconciled: the Kendall-tau monotonicity study with bootstrap significance testing, the demonstration that radar is necessary (replacing radar with learnable points costs ~28% MAE), and the observation that lidar-style depth completion (BPNet, NLSPN) transfers poorly to sparse radar (Tab. 7).

Backbone-matched comparisons are persuasive where they are given: on ZJU, POLAR with UniDepth (629.6 MAE) substantially beats RadarCam-Depth with the same UniDepth backbone (1152.5 MAE), indicating the polynomial fitting itself, and not only the MDE prior, drives the gain.

The paper is clearly written and the geometric intuition (a monotone polynomial has inflection points, unlike an affine map, so it can stretch/compress different depth intervals) is presented pedagogically well, with readable figures.
weaknesses: Central claim versus actual capability: the transformation is a single global function of the scaleless depth, d̂(x,y) = Σ ĉ_i z(x,y)^i, whose coefficients are produced from a globally pooled feature vector, and the proposed regularizer explicitly penalizes order inversions (||1 − dd̂/dz||₁). Such a monotone function of z cannot change the relative depth ordering of any two pixels. Yet the abstract, intro, and Fig. 1 motivate the method precisely by 'objects placed at incorrect relative depths' and 'cross-region misalignments' that a scale-and-shift cannot reconcile. POLAR can only correct errors that are a monotone function of the predicted depth; the paper never establishes that the residual MDE error has this structure (the scatter in Fig. 3 shows large spread at fixed z, i.e. a large non-functional component). This is a mismatch between the headline 'fundamental insight' and what the method can do.

Internally inconsistent reported results, which directly affect the SOTA claim. Table 1 lists ZJU 50 m POLAR = 578.0/1108.6, but Tab. 9 gives 629.6/1171.3 for the best (UniDepth) configuration and 640.3–707.1 for the others; Table 1 lists VoD POLAR = 1293.7/2420.6, while Tab. 10's best is 1500.1 (UniDepth) / 1770.5 (Depth Anything). No appendix configuration reproduces the main-table numbers, and the difference is never explained.

The headline improvement percentages are inconsistent and not traceable to the tables: the abstract claims 'an average of 24.9% in MAE and 33.2% in RMSE', the introduction claims '29.1%', and Sec. 4.1 reports 4.4%/3.7% on nuScenes, 38.5%/57.5% on ZJU and 31.8%/38.5% on VoD. A direct recomputation against Table 1/7 (e.g. vs. TacoDepth on nuScenes: 1046.8→1014.4 MAE = 3.1%, 2487.5→2475.7 RMSE = 0.5%) matches none of the quoted averages. This is not a cosmetic issue: the paper's central selling point is the magnitude of the improvement.

On the primary benchmark the margin is marginal and within run-to-run noise: nuScenes 50 m 1014.4 vs. 1046.8 MAE and 2475.7 vs. 2487.5 RMSE over TacoDepth (0.5% RMSE). This is hard to reconcile with the qualitative claim (Fig. 4) that RadarCam-Depth 'fail[s] to reconstruct entire regions' and with the qualitative panels, given the near-identical RMSE on that dataset.

The key 'polynomial beats affine' evidence is unconvincing. In Tab. 5 the degree-1 (scale+shift) configuration reaches 2156.8 MAE at 50 m, which is worse than the raw UniDepth prediction (2129.8, Tab. 4) even though the backbone is frozen and a learned affine should at least be able to reproduce the raw prediction. This suggests the affine baseline is under-trained/under-specified, which inflates the apparent benefit of higher degrees. Likewise, the isotonic/spline/'learnable points' comparisons in Tab. 13 are not matched in capacity or objective to POLAR, so 'learning mitigates radar noise' is under-supported.

Architecture and narrative do not match: the fused representation S ∈ R^{H×W×c_s}, which is described as encoding 'spatial correspondences between radar and MDE features', is reduced by global average pooling to a single vector before the MLP predicts the N+1 coefficients. All spatial structure in the fusion is therefore discarded; only global scene statistics can influence the output. The prototype-based radar aggregation and cross-modal attention are consequently hard to justify as necessary, and the spatial-correspondence claim is not supported by the design.

The efficiency claim needs qualification: it is not stated whether the (frozen) MDE backbone forward pass is included in POLAR's 24.81 ms / 89.70 GFLOPs, nor whether baselines' backbones are counted on the same basis. Since the 40 fps / real-time claim hinges on this, the comparison is currently ambiguous. The theoretical content is also thin: Prop. 1 (three (d̂,d) pairs cannot be fit by one affine) is elementary, and the Corollary's claim of 'arbitrarily well' approximation by a Taylor expansion assumes precisely what is in question (that d is a function of d̂) and conflates local Taylor approximation with a globally fit low-degree polynomial. Finally, novelty is modest — a 2-parameter affine head replaced by an (N+1)-parameter polynomial head, with standard radar aggregation/fusion components.
